source: PRISM: Lee, Kang, Shin (2026) Make LLMs See Like Investigators, Not Just Think More (ACL 2026)
finding: Four-agent pipeline on MuSR murder mysteries: evidence filter, Motive-Means-Opportunity profiles, an ACH matrix, then a judge. Beat plain prompting on all 10 models.
numbers: 250 MuSR murder-mystery questions, two suspects each, 10 LLMs (GPT-5.2 plus 9 open models, 8B-70B), temperature 0. Direct 58.1% mean, PRISM 71.3% (+13.2 points). Range of gain +6.0 (Ministral-8B) to +22.0 (GPT-5.2: 58.0 to 80.0).
limits: Whole pipeline, not ACH alone. Two-suspect task is easy to matrix. One benchmark. Single run at temperature 0, no confidence intervals reported.
agent_relevance: The full structured pipeline helps; the next lines show which part did the work.
quote: improvement was observed without exception across all 10 models

source: PRISM ablation (Lee et al. 2026), ACH stage alone
finding: Removing the ACH matrix stage costs almost nothing. The gain comes from filtering evidence and from the motive-means-opportunity profile, not from the hypothesis-by-evidence matrix.
numbers: Evidence filter plus judge only (P1P4): 63.8%. Add MMO profiles (P1P2P4): 70.5% (+6.7). Add ACH matrix (full): 71.3% (+0.8, 11% of the 7.5-point gain). MMO is 89% of the structuring gain.
limits: +0.8 is an average over 10 models with no significance test. ACH comes last in the chain, so it sees already structured profiles. Authors still defend it as bias suppression for ambiguous cases, not shown by data.
agent_relevance: Direct support for schema 4b: a full matrix adds under 1 point once evidence is filtered and a per-suspect structure exists.

source: PRISM general-purpose baselines (Lee et al. 2026)
finding: Telling models to think step by step or act like a detective did nothing on culprit inference. Self-consistency helped a bit.
numbers: Direct 58.1%, CoT 57.2%, Persona 58.2%, Persona+CoT 58.0%, Self-Consistency (5 samples, T=0.7) 63.2% (+5.1). CoT hurt: Mixtral-8x7B -4.8, Qwen3-14B -2.0, Llama-3.1-8B large drop.
limits: Same single benchmark. CoT harm is model specific.
agent_relevance: Matches schema 4b row on slow-down prompts. Evidence filtering alone (63.8%) beat SC (63.2%) with one pass.
quote: simply instructing to 'think more' has limitations

source: PRISM scale and ensembles (Lee et al. 2026, appendix D)
finding: Gain is the same for small and large models. Mixing models or adding debate did not beat the best single model with PRISM.
numbers: Small (8B-14B) mean 70.2%, large (27B-70B) 70.6%; gain +12.2 in both. Best single (GPT-5.2 + PRISM) 80.0%; Top-3 ensemble 78.4%, Top-5 77.2%, all-10 76.0%, Hierarchical Review 78.0%, Structured Debate 77.6%.
limits: Ensemble is not a full test of debate. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate) and shows structure beats model size. Plain GPT-5.2 ranked only 5th of 10 (58.0%) yet topped the board once structured.

source: Zhong et al. (2026) Before the Action: Benchmarking LLMs on Prospective Hypothesis Discovery (HypoArena)
finding: Benchmark of 988 cases in six domains where models must build a grounded, discriminative hypothesis set from inconclusive evidence. Tests a baseline single pass against an Agent mode with 12 structured analytic skills including ACH.
numbers: 15 LLMs, pairwise LLM judge (seed-2.0-pro) with Bradley-Terry-Davidson ratings; 1,500 pairwise expert comparisons gave Kendall tau 0.90, Spearman 0.98 with the judge. Baseline leaderboard spans over 360 rating points; top three are claude-sonnet-4.6, claude-opus-4.6, gpt-5.4.
limits: Judge is an LLM. Tasks are hypothesis generation, not choosing among given hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Closest modern test of a SAT skill library inside an LLM agent.

source: Zhong et al. (2026) HypoArena, Agent mode vs baseline
finding: Giving models the structured analytic skill library (ACH, chronology, assumptions check and others) gave no uniform gain. Effects ranged from big gain to big loss and did not track model strength.
numbers: Per-model change in arena rating: kimi-k2.5 +88 (best), claude-opus-4.6 about -58 to -60 (worst), others between. Spearman between baseline strength and change: -0.10. One named failure mode: candidate compression (rich intermediate analysis squeezed into a narrow final set).
limits: Skills are chosen and chained by the model; the ACH skill is not isolated. Rating points are relative to a pool.
agent_relevance: A skill library with ACH can hurt the strongest model. Supports 4b: do not add an ACH step without a measured test per model.
quote: Agent mode does not provide uniform gains

source: Zhong et al. (2026) HypoArena skill definition for ACH (appendix K)
finding: The ACH skill used is an evidence-diagnosticity matrix with C/I/NA scoring ranked by inconsistency (least disconfirming evidence wins), run as one skill in a sequential pipeline.
numbers: Library has 12 skills; baseline is single-pass generation. No ablation of ACH alone is reported.
limits: No isolated ACH ablation.
agent_relevance: Shows how a modern agent harness encodes Heuer's rule; also shows no one tested it by itself.

source: AgentCDM: Zhao et al. (2025) Enhancing Multi-Agent Collaborative Decision-Making via ACH-Inspired Structured Reasoning
finding: Decision agent evaluates other agents' answers as competing hypotheses, with a two-stage trained scaffold (RL with GRPO, scaffold faded in stage two). Zero-shot ACH prompting gave small gains; training gave large gains.
numbers: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, ARC-Challenge, four base models. All-average (garbled table): single agent 66.0; unstructured informed-dictator 65.8; ACH prompt homogeneous 67.9 (+2.0), Qwen-7B-Instruct as ACH decider 67.5 (+1.6), Qwen-7B-R1 74.5 (+8.6), AgentCDM 77.5 (+11.6). Text: ACH prompt beats unstructured decider by 1.9 points.
limits: Table extraction is messy; read as approximate. Trained model, so gain mixes RL with ACH wording. No ACH-vs-neutral-structure control. Cooperative agents only.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot ACH-style prompt adds about 2 points on multiple choice; most gain needs training, which our agent does not do.

source: AgentCDM ablation (Zhao et al. 2025)
finding: Keeping the rigid ACH scaffold in training hurt generalisation: scaffold-only was worse than a plain prompt.
numbers: Accuracy MMLU / MMLU-Pro / ARC-C: Full 78.5 / 65.2 / 96.0; vanilla prompt 72.6 / 52.5 / 89.0; scaffolding-only 68.1 / 49.4 / 84.0; exploration-only 71.5 / 52.1 / 89.7.
limits: Author interpretation, one training recipe.
agent_relevance: Rigid ACH protocol below the plain prompt by 4.5 points on MMLU and 3.1 on MMLU-Pro. A fixed matrix can lower accuracy.
quote: rigid adherence to the structured protocol impairs generalization

source: AgentCDM scaling by agent count (Zhao et al. 2025)
finding: With capable models (GPT-4) more input agents helped; with weak models (Mistral-7B) more agents lowered accuracy because noise outweighed signal.
numbers: MMLU-Pro, figure only; no exact numbers read.
limits: Numbers were in a figure; direction only.
agent_relevance: Weighing many weak hypotheses via a judge can amplify noise.

source: Evron (2026) Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
finding: Design paper that scales ACH from a handful to thousands of machine-checkable hypotheses ('brains'), with an LLM turning reports into brains, judging matches and running an update loop.
numbers: No accuracy results; no benchmark. Cites Heuer that more than seven hypotheses may be unmanageable for a person.
limits: Concept only, no evaluation (checked text for results).
agent_relevance: Shows ACH used as a continuous matching loop; the limit on hypothesis count is a human limit, not a machine one. Untested.
quote: more than seven hypotheses may be unmanageable

source: Coulthart, Keller, Young (2023) What ChatGPT can and cannot do for intelligence (Lawfare)
finding: Gave GPT-4 Heuer's eight ACH steps for 'Will Russia use nuclear weapons in Ukraine?' with supplied context. It made three hypotheses and an evidence matrix, judged 'bargaining tool' most likely.
numbers: No numbers. One question, one run. Authors call it a preliminary test; output rated as a first draft from an entry-level analyst.
limits: Anecdote, no ground truth, model lacked post-2021 knowledge so context was injected by hand. Authors warn the model bridges gaps with plausible but wrong content.
agent_relevance: Shows the matrix can be produced on demand; says nothing about accuracy.

source: Roberts (2025) LLM SATs FTW, as summarised on mattdot sats4llms
finding: Practitioner ACH tool: query 1 makes hypotheses; one query per hypothesis for evidence for and against; one query per hypothesis-evidence pair scores -5 to +5; code totals scores; human edits. Claim: a single zero-shot prompt fails.
numbers: No accuracy numbers. Stack: GPT-4, LangChain, Pydantic, Streamlit.
limits: Claim that single-prompt ACH fails is the page author's reading; no controlled test was reported.
agent_relevance: Matrix filled cell by cell with separate calls and summed in code is the common pattern; cost grows with cells.

source: suprathermal (2024) ACH-Grounding, as summarised on mattdot sats4llms
finding: Open-source tool where the LLM only fills cells and deterministic code does the likelihood synthesis. Token cost grows as (evidence + hypotheses) squared.
numbers: No benchmark results reported. Cites arXiv 2401.11817 and 2508.01781 on hallucination bounds.
limits: Practical only for few hypotheses and a few uncertain evidence items, by the page's own account.
agent_relevance: Splitting model judgment from arithmetic is sound engineering but untested here.

source: Aperstein, Remez, Apartsin (2026) EMR-ACH: Evidence Matrix Reasoning (draft)
finding: Draft that frames ACH as evidence-matrix inference for forecasting (ForecastBench, GDELT-CAMEO, earnings) and compares to CoT, RAG, self-consistency, debate, Tree-of-Thoughts, Reflexion. All method results still TBD.
numbers: Only pilot numbers (N=79 ForecastBench): direct and CoT collapsed to near-constant No (recall No about 0.96, Yes about 0.17) and did not beat majority class (83.4% accuracy). Full set 6,294 forecasts.
limits: No results to cite; pilot is legacy framing and not comparable. Authors admit no calibration test.
agent_relevance: Watch for results. A strong majority-class baseline (83.4%) makes accuracy gains hard to show.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: 11 LLMs on a Wason 2-4-6 style rule-discovery game show confirmation bias: they test cases that fit their guess. More disconfirming tests go with more success.
numbers: Task success 6% to 78% within 45 turns. Positive correlation between disconfirm:confirm test ratio (I:C) and success, significant in both thinking and non-thinking groups; 80 episodes per model-variant. Earlier work cited: best 26% success.
limits: Number-triple game, not intelligence analysis. Thinking mode raised success without a consistent rise in I:C.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLMs need pushing toward disconfirming tests, which is the part of ACH that matters.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) interventions
finding: Two human debiasing prompts, Think-in-Opposites and Dual-Goal, raised rule discovery on average from 42% to 56%. Gains were significant for thinking models and mixed for non-thinking models.
numbers: Think-in-Opposites raised success in all 11 model settings; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11 and hurt non-thinking models (for example Qwen3-14B non-thinking 0.23 to 0.13, Qwen3-32B 0.33 to 0.10). I:C rose in 18 of 22 cases. Distilling the behaviour transferred to a Blicket test.
limits: Qwen/Llama/R1 family only. Dual-Goal drops in non-thinking mode are model-specific.
agent_relevance: A targeted 'test the opposite' move helps where a generic matrix is not tested. Narrow counterexample to the blanket debiasing row in 4b; works only in reasoning models.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench
finding: 12 LLMs play a Wason-style rule-discovery game. Reasoning models do better; the main driver is negative testing (trying cases outside the current guess).
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Confirmation bias vs success Spearman -0.779 (p=0.003); confirmation bias vs conclusive falsification rate -0.937 (p<0.001). Falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%.
limits: 12 models, one game family. Authors note negative testing is not always the best move.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as above: disconfirming tests are what pay, not tabulating consistency.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator (Solution Investigator Agent)
finding: Agent that keeps a shared state of competing hypotheses, a counterfactual challenger and cited evidence for technical diagnosis. Final mean 79.2/100 vs 67.3 for a direct answer.
numbers: 303 forum-thread corpus, 100 evaluation cases, Gemini backbone. Final scores: direct (BAS) 67.3, think-about-competing-explanations (THK) 67.5, THK-interactive 72.8, Ask-5 72.3, ReAct 69.0, Tree-of-Thoughts 61.5, SIA 79.2 [72.7, 83.7].
limits: LLM rubric evaluator. Single domain family. SIA also asks more questions (5.2 vs 3.7).
agent_relevance: Key: merely prompting the model to analyse competing explanations (THK 67.5) gave +0.2 over direct. Gains came from asking discriminating questions.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) SIA ablation and stress test
finding: Dropping structured investigation or counterfactual critique costs most. Evidence-based weight updates (the ACH-like scoring step) matter least.
numbers: Full 79.2. Without structured investigation 72.8; without counterfactual critique 74.0; without follow-up questions 75.0; without hypothesis expansion 76.5 (pool potential 89.2 to 79.3); without final adjudication 76.0; without weight updates 78.5 (-0.7). A wrong user suggestion: final 80.0 to 76.0 on 10 paired cases; wrong cause chosen 2/10.
limits: 10 paired cases is tiny. Same single-domain data.
agent_relevance: Weights on evidence cost -0.7 when removed, in line with PRISM's +0.8 for ACH. Candidate generation and discriminating questions carry the gain. Also shows anchoring to a planted wrong hypothesis.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) other backbones
finding: Advantage holds on other model backbones at a lower level.
numbers: GPT-5.6 Terra: SIA 75.4 vs THK-int 69.2 (+6.2). Claude Sonnet 5: SIA 76.1 vs THK-int 68.4 (+7.7).
limits: Single run per cell reported; no pooled test.
agent_relevance: The gap from interactive, hypothesis-tracking structure is stable across model families.

source: Zeng, Zhang, Zhang (2026) EviDx: Evidence-Aware Active Diagnosis with Scaffolded LLM Agents
finding: Clinical agent with evidence states, role agents and an observer that blocks termination until uncertainty is low and evidence coverage met. Competing diagnoses are tracked.
numbers: Multiple-choice accuracy: Claude Sonnet 4.6 66% on JAMA and 52% on DiagnosisArena; Qwen3-8B 18% to 44% on JAMA; Llama3.1-8B 17% to 31%. 100 cases per dataset; observer-specific gains smaller and model-dependent; open-ended diagnosis near 0% for small models.
limits: Not a pure ACH test; scaffold bundles tools, roles and termination control. Gains clearest on multiple choice. Small models' evidence recall fell (Llama3.1-8B 63.8% to 15.1%).
agent_relevance: Process control (do not stop early) did the work, not a matrix. Links to termination guardrails.

source: Liu, Neubig, Andreas (2024) An Incomplete Loop: Deductive, Inductive and Abductive Reasoning in LMs (COLM)
finding: Models generate n=5 hypotheses for a rule and rerank them by verbalised confidence, likelihood of the data, or an external validator. Reranking with confidence and log-probability gave similar gains.
numbers: Four LMs (GPT and Llama), linear functions, an invented-language task and Kalamang. Abstract: LMs sometimes infer useful descriptions but fail to learn from human ones; strong dissociation between reasoning types. No improvement in Kalamang for most settings.
limits: Not intelligence analysis; hypotheses are rules, not events. Exact accuracy table not read.
agent_relevance: Generate-several-then-score-fit works on formal tasks and not on real-world messy ones.

source: Cheikes, Brown, Lehner, Adelman (2004) Confirmation Bias in Complex Analyses (MITRE)
finding: Search-result summary only (full text blocked, 403): ACH reduced confirmation bias only for participants without professional analysis experience; bias appeared as weighting, not interpretation.
numbers: Not read; no numbers verified.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a pointer, to be checked by the human-study angle.
agent_relevance: Weighting is the very step an LLM matrix fills in.

source: Pirolli and Good (2004) Evaluation of a Computer Support Tool for Analysis of Competing Hypotheses
finding: Older software ACH workspace compared with and without the tool; known only from a search listing. Server refused connection.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Oldest computational ACH support; results unverified.
